panels.title: Jobs outstanding
panels.description: By state. `blocked` is waiting on a dependency - a manifest whose blobs have not landed - and a large blocked count with an empty pending one usually means a dependency graph that never resolves rather than a busy fleet. Settled jobs are deliberately not here: they are counted, not gauged, because archiving old rows would otherwise read as work being undone.

panels.title: Oldest job still waiting
panels.description: THE ONE TO ALERT ON. Flat in a moving queue however deep it is, climbing minute for minute in a stalled one. If this is rising while `leased` above is zero, no worker is taking work - check the fleet row below before looking at the queue at all.

panels.title: Bytes outstanding
panels.description: How much is actually left, which a job count cannot say: a queue of nine manifests and one 23 GB blob is one job from done and hours from finished. `pending` is the planned size of what has not started; `in_flight` is what leased jobs have moved so far.

panels.title: Work that is paused
panels.description: Outstanding jobs whose transfer somebody paused. Read beside the depth panel: a deep queue that is paused is a decision, and a deep queue that is not is an incident. Without this they look identical.

panels.title: Throughput
panels.description: Bytes per second. `transferred` crossed the wire; `saved` is what a dedupe or a server-side mount meant nobody had to move. Kept apart because adding them together reports bandwidth nobody used - and because the saved line is the measure of whether this system is earning its keep.

panels.title: Jobs settled per second
panels.description: Terminal outcomes only. A failure with attempts left went back on the queue and is still outstanding work - it is counted by the depth panel above and by the failure panel below, not here. Without that distinction one bad afternoon at a registry reads as hundreds of permanent failures.

panels.title: How long a job takes (p95)
panels.description: First lease to completion, by kind. A manifest is metadata and should be sub-second; a blob is however large it is, so this line tracks the size of what is being moved as much as the speed of moving it. A sudden rise on manifests alone is the registry, not the network.

panels.title: Failures by class, retried or not
panels.description: Every failure, including the ones that were retried and then succeeded - which is the point. A class whose retries are climbing is a dependency degrading before it breaks, and it is invisible on the settled-outcome panel because the job eventually worked. `auth` is a credential nobody rotated; `transient` is a registry having a bad day; `digest_mismatch` is corruption.

panels.title: Workers
panels.description: By state. `stale` is a worker that stopped heartbeating - its leases will be reaped and its jobs redone, so a persistent stale count is work being repeated rather than lost. By state and never by worker id: a worker id is a pod name, and pod names are unbounded over a cluster's life.

panels.title: Fleet concurrency
panels.description: Three lines and two gaps, and the gaps are the diagnosis. `granted` below `max` is the budget controller holding back because a vendor registry is struggling. `active` at `granted` with a deep queue is the fleet being the bottleneck - add workers. `active` well below `granted` with a deep queue is neither, and means work is blocked rather than waiting.

panels.title: Transfers not yet settled
panels.description: The transfers page, aggregated. A transfer wedged in `planning` or `verifying` has no jobs in the queue at all, so it is invisible on every panel above - this is the only place it shows.

panels.title: Are the queue gauges trustworthy
panels.description: Failed samples per second. On a failed sample the gauges above KEEP their previous values rather than dropping to zero, because a frozen zero reads as an empty queue - the one thing a measurement failure must never say. Non-zero here means everything on this dashboard is stale.
